section.title: Cyrus, the Lord's Anointed
section.sectionRationale: This passage contains one of the boldest predictive claims in all of Scripture: the LORD names Cyrus by name as His anointed shepherd who will rebuild Jerusalem and free the exiles, more than a century before Cyrus was born. It presses to its sharpest point the Book of Comfort's whole argument that only the true God can declare the end from the beginning, and it closes with an astonishing invitation for every nation on earth to turn to Him and be saved.
section.thesis: The LORD who alone declares the end from the beginning names a pagan king, Cyrus, as His anointed instrument to free His exiled people and rebuild His city, proving there is no God besides Him, and He caps this proof with an open invitation for every knee on earth to bow to Him alone.
section.frameNote: Eight movements: the LORD as maker of all things who confirms His servants' words; the naming of Cyrus as shepherd even before his birth; the LORD's grasp of Cyrus's right hand to subdue nations; Cyrus called by name though he does not know the LORD; the folly of the clay quarreling with its potter; nations submitting and confessing God is with Israel alone; the LORD's open, undisguised speech; and the climactic invitation for all the earth to turn and be saved.

units.label: The LORD who made all things

verses.text: Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer who formed you from the womb: “I am the LORD, who has made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who by Myself spread out the earth,
who foils the signs of false prophets and makes fools of diviners, who confounds the wise and turns their knowledge into nonsense,

who confirms the message of His servant and fulfills the counsel of His messengers, who says of Jerusalem, ‘She will be inhabited,’ and of the cities of Judah, ‘They will be rebuilt, and I will restore their ruins,’

units.label: Who says of Cyrus, My shepherd

verses.text: who says to the depths of the sea, ‘Be dry, and I will dry up your currents,’
who says of Cyrus, ‘My shepherd will fulfill all that I desire,’ who says of Jerusalem, ‘She will be rebuilt,’ and of the temple, ‘Let its foundation be laid.’”

This is what the LORD says to Cyrus His {{mashiach|anointed}}, whose right hand I have grasped to subdue nations before him, to disarm kings, to open the doors before him, so that the gates will not be shut:
“I will go before you and level the mountains; I will break down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron.
I will give you the treasures of darkness and the riches hidden in secret places, so that you may know that I am the LORD, the God of Israel, who calls you by name.

units.label: For the sake of Jacob My servant
units.note: though you have not known Me

verses.text: For the sake of Jacob My servant and Israel My chosen one, I call you by name; I have given you a title of honor, though you have not known Me.
I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me. I will equip you for battle, though you have not known Me,
so that all may know, from where the sun rises to where it sets, that there is none but Me; I am the LORD, and there is no other.
I form the light and create the darkness; I bring prosperity and create calamity. I, the LORD, do all these things.

units.label: Woe to him who quarrels with his Maker

verses.text: Drip down, O heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness. Let the earth open up that salvation may sprout and righteousness spring up with it; I, the LORD, have created it.
Woe to him who quarrels with his {{yotser|Maker}}, one clay pot among many. Does the clay ask the potter, ‘What are you making?’ Does your work say, ‘He has no hands’?
Woe to him who says to his father, ‘What have you begotten?’ or to his mother, ‘What have you brought forth?’”
Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and its Maker: “How dare you question Me about My sons, or instruct Me in the work of My hands?
It is I who made the earth and created man upon it. It was My hands that stretched out the heavens, and I ordained all their host.
I will raise up Cyrus in righteousness, and I will make all his ways straight. He will rebuild My city and set My exiles free, but not for payment or reward, says the LORD of Hosts.”

units.label: Nations will come over to you

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “The products of Egypt and the merchandise of Cush, along with the Sabeans, men of stature, will come over to you and will be yours; they will trudge behind you; they will come over in chains and bow down to you. They will confess to you: ‘God is indeed with you, and there is no other; there is no other God.’”
Truly You are a God who hides Himself, O God of Israel, the Savior.
They will all be put to shame and humiliated; the makers of idols will depart together in disgrace.
But Israel will be saved by the LORD with an everlasting salvation; you will not be put to shame or humiliated, to ages everlasting.

units.label: I have not spoken in secret

verses.text: For thus says the LORD, who created the heavens, He is God; He formed the earth and fashioned it; He established it; He did not create it to be empty, but formed it to be inhabited: “I am the LORD, and there is no other.
I have not spoken in secret, from a place in a land of darkness. I did not say to the descendants of Jacob, ‘Seek Me in a wasteland.’ I, the LORD, speak the truth; I say what is right.

units.label: Turn to Me and be saved

verses.text: Come, gather together, and draw near, you fugitives from the nations. Ignorant are those who carry idols of wood and pray to a god that cannot save.

Speak up and present your case, yes, let them take counsel together. Who foretold this long ago? Who announced it from ancient times? Was it not I, the LORD? There is no other God but Me, a righteous God and Savior; there is none but Me.
Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.
By Myself I have sworn; truth has gone out from My mouth, a word that will not be revoked: Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance.
Surely they will say of Me, ‘In the LORD alone are righteousness and strength.’” All who rage against Him will come to Him and be put to shame.
In the LORD all descendants of Israel will be justified and will exult.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one, one set apart and empowered for a God-given task, the same word that becomes the title Messiah. It is striking that Isaiah applies this word to Cyrus, a pagan Persian king who does not know the LORD, showing that God can anoint even an unbelieving ruler as His chosen instrument, while the fullest and final Anointed One remains Jesus the Christ.

yotser.gloss: Potter, one who forms or shapes, from the verb yatsar, to form or fashion, the same word used of God forming Adam from the dust. The image of the clay quarreling with its potter exposes the absurdity of any creature questioning its Maker's right to shape history, including raising up a foreign king for His own redemptive purposes.

basic.context: In one of the most striking predictive claims in the Bible, the LORD names Cyrus, a Persian king who would not be born for roughly another hundred and fifty years, calling him His shepherd and even His anointed, the one who will free the exiles and see Jerusalem and its temple rebuilt. The passage builds this astonishing claim into an argument that only the true God can declare the future, closing with an open invitation for every nation on earth to turn to Him and be saved.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage names Cyrus with startling specificity long before his birth, and Cyrus's later decree, recorded in Ezra 1:1-4, releasing the Jewish exiles to return and rebuild the temple, matches this prophecy closely. The chapter's repeated insistence that the LORD alone declares the end from the beginning is the very claim this specific, named prophecy is meant to prove beyond doubt.
basic.originalLanguages: Remarkably, Cyrus is called the LORD's {{mashiach}}, anointed one, though he was a pagan king who, the text says twice, did not know the LORD, showing that God's anointing can rest even on someone outside the covenant to accomplish His purposes for His people. The image of the clay questioning the {{yotser}}, potter, underscores that no creature, and no foreign king, has standing to challenge the Maker's right to direct history as He wills.
basic.typology: Cyrus, an anointed deliverer who frees captives and enables the rebuilding of God's city though he is not himself part of God's covenant people, foreshadows in a partial and imperfect way the true and final Anointed One, Jesus the Messiah, who accomplishes a far greater deliverance and gathers a people not limited to any one nation. The invitation for all the ends of the earth to turn and be saved, verse 22, anticipates the global reach of the gospel.
basic.christ: Paul directly applies Isaiah 45:23, 'every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance,' to Jesus Christ in Philippians 2:10-11, declaring that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow and every tongue confess Him as Lord, identifying Jesus fully with the LORD who speaks these words. Cyrus, though merely a human instrument and not himself a believer, becomes an unlikely, partial picture of the Anointed One who frees captives, while Jesus alone is the true Messiah in whom this passage's invitation to all the earth is fully realized.
basic.god: God governs history so completely that He can name a specific foreign king more than a century before his birth and call him His own shepherd and anointed, even though that king does not know Him. He is also the potter with sovereign right over every part of His creation, and He is, remarkably, a God who hides Himself yet still speaks plainly and truly, inviting the whole earth, not Israel alone, to turn to Him and be saved.
basic.crossReferences: Ezra 1:1-4 records Cyrus's actual decree freeing the exiles and funding the temple's rebuilding, fulfilling this prophecy. Philippians 2:10-11 applies Isaiah 45:23 directly to Jesus, every knee bowing and every tongue confessing Him as Lord. Romans 14:11 also quotes this verse regarding final accountability before God. Ezra 1:1 itself explicitly credits the LORD with stirring Cyrus's spirit to fulfill Isaiah's word.
basic.oneStory: This passage's astonishing naming of Cyrus, and the LORD's claim to be the only one who can declare the end from the beginning, becomes the platform for an invitation that reaches beyond Israel to all the ends of the earth. That invitation, and the verse that seals it, is applied directly to Jesus in the New Testament, showing that the God who directed a pagan king's rise is the same Lord before whom every knee will one day bow.

context.literary:
This long oracle is shaped like a pair of bookends around a single stunning address. It opens with a chain of seven or more clauses beginning 'who,' all hanging on the same speaker: 'I am the LORD, who has made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens,' 44:24, and the chain runs on through false prophets, the servant's word, Jerusalem and the sea until it arrives at its goal, 'who says of Cyrus, "My shepherd,"' 44:28. Everything before Cyrus's name is the build-up, a list of what only the Creator can do, and the name falls at the end of the list like the resolution of a long sentence.

Chapter 45 then turns from speaking about Cyrus to speaking to him. Verses 1 to 7 are a rare thing in the Bible, an oracle addressed in the second person to a foreign king, who will never read it. The real audience is the exiles listening in. The oracle is knit together by a single word, to know. The LORD acts 'so that you may know that I am the LORD,' verse 3, though Cyrus 'has not known Me,' verses 4 and 5, so that 'all may know, from where the sun rises to where it sets,' verse 6. Cyrus is the means, and the knowledge of God by every nation is the end.

The rest alternates between challenge and invitation. A short hymn in verse 8 prays for righteousness and salvation to sprout like a crop. Two woe oracles in verses 9 to 13 answer the grumbling of those who cannot see how a pagan could be God's instrument, and they end by restating the commission. Verses 14 to 17 turn to the nations who come over in chains and confess, and to the quiet exclamation of verse 15. The last section, verses 18 to 25, is a trial speech: the fugitives of the nations are called to court, the question of who foretold this is asked, and the verdict of verse 22, 'Turn to Me and be saved,' leads straight into an oath. The refrain 'I am the LORD, and there is no other' is repeated, with small variations, in verses 5, 6, 14, 18, 21 and 22, until it becomes the voice of the whole piece. Both halves are fenced by creation: the speech begins with the Maker of all things in 44:24 and ends its main argument with the Creator who did not make the earth empty, 45:18.
context.historical:
Cyrus II of Persia rose with astonishing speed. By the middle of the sixth century BC he had overthrown the Median king and absorbed his empire, he defeated the wealthy Lydian kingdom in the west, and in October 539 BC Babylon itself fell to him, by the usual accounts with very little fighting. Later Greek writers say the Persians entered along the bed of the Euphrates, which fits the picture of gates that 'will not be shut,' 45:1, and a fortified city that was nevertheless opened. The vast treasure that came into his hands lies behind 'the treasures of darkness and the riches hidden in secret places,' 45:3, though the text does not tie itself to a single capture.

The policy that followed is the practical background to 44:28 and 45:13. Cyrus returned displaced peoples and their gods to their homelands and supported their sanctuaries. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay barrel from Babylon, records this policy in Babylonian terms and credits the god Marduk. It does not mention Jerusalem or the Jews, so it illustrates the kind of policy Cyrus followed and does not itself confirm the Jewish decree. That decree is preserved in the Bible: a Hebrew proclamation in Ezra 1:1-4 and an Aramaic memorandum in Ezra 6:3-5, which orders the house of God rebuilt, gives its dimensions, and says that the cost is to come from the royal treasury and the temple vessels are to be returned. The first group of returnees was led by a figure called Sheshbazzar, Ezra 1:8 and 5:14-16.

For the exiles, the prophecy stood in a tradition. Jeremiah had said that after seventy years Babylon would be dealt with and the people brought back, Jeremiah 29:10, and Ezra 1:1 says the proclamation was in fulfilment of that word. The rhetorical challenge of the chapter, who foretold this long ago, was addressed to a people who could place the prophecy in their own scrolls and watch it become history. Josephus reports a tradition that Cyrus was shown this passage; the report comes from centuries later and cannot be checked, but it shows how the connection was understood.
context.canonical:
Cyrus appears in more than one place in the Old Testament. The Chronicler ends his history with Cyrus's proclamation, 2 Chronicles 36:22-23, and Ezra begins with the same words, Ezra 1:1-3, so the Hebrew Bible closes and the second chapter of Israel's life opens on the same hinge. Daniel records that he prospered 'during the reign of Cyrus the Persian,' Daniel 6:28. Within Isaiah itself the foreshadowing is in 41:2 and 41:25 and in the summons of 'a bird of prey from the east' in 46:11, and the pattern is brought back in 48:14-15.

The title 'shepherd' belongs in a larger family of images, because the kings of Israel and the LORD Himself are called shepherds. The tragedy of Ezekiel 34 is the failure of Israel's shepherds, and the answer of Ezekiel 34:23 is a single shepherd, David, who will tend them. Jesus applies the title to Himself, John 10:11. Isaiah 45:1 stands in an odd place in that sequence, since the shepherd of the exile is a foreigner.

One of the most used verses of this passage in the New Testament is 45:23. Paul quotes it in Romans 14:11, with the beginning of the verse, 'As surely as I live,' folded in from other texts, as a warning that every person will give an account to God. In Philippians 2:9-11 he draws on the same verse to say that every knee should bow 'at the name of Jesus.' The Letter to the Hebrews points to the oath of verse 23 when it says that God swore by Himself, Hebrews 6:13. Paul's claim that God is both 'just and the one who justifies,' Romans 3:26, echoes 45:21, where He is 'a righteous God and Savior,' and Paul's use of the potter in Romans 9:20-21 draws on 45:9, as the BSB footnote on that verse records.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet wants to change what the exiles think the story is about. They saw a catastrophe, Babylon rising and Judah falling, and a second rising of Persia that might be a mere change of masters. He tells them that the whole sequence has one author. The Persian conqueror is a tool in the hand of the God whom Cyrus does not know, and every step of the exile and the release is in the plan. The intent is to place a defeated people under a sovereign who was not surprised, and to make them able to trust Him through a coming change that would seem to them political rather than divine.

A second purpose sits inside the first. The oracle is built to be overheard. By speaking directly to Cyrus, who is not in the room, the prophet makes the exiles listen to what God says to the world, and what God says is not primarily about Israel's advantage. Verses 6 and 22 are explicit: the purpose is that all may know and that all the ends of the earth may turn. The prophet wants the hearers to see that their release is a message to the nations and a part of an invitation, and that a nation chosen for a purpose cannot keep God to itself.

The woe oracles of verses 9 to 13 reveal a third purpose. Some of the exiles were offended that God would use a pagan. The prophet takes that offence head on and says that the Maker does not need their approval for His choice of instrument. The aim is to turn complaint into trust.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a unique act, the naming of a particular king, and it does not prescribe that believers should expect names of future rulers. Nor does it tell us that every ruler who does something favourable to the church is God's anointed in the sense Cyrus was. The text reports that God used Cyrus for a purpose; it does not say Cyrus was right with God. It says plainly that he did not know the LORD, verses 4 and 5.

The passage does prescribe a posture. The woe on those who quarrel with the Maker, verses 9 to 11, is a warning against the kind of complaint that demands that God explain Himself before it will trust Him. The invitation of verse 22 is a command and a promise at once, and it applies to every reader: turn and be saved. And the verses on the nations' confession give believers the model of the hope that people of every kind will come.

The claim in verse 7, that God creates calamity, describes His sovereignty over the events of history. It does not give any individual reader a verdict on the cause of a particular disaster, and the book of Job is a standing warning against that move.

debates.question: How should we understand Cyrus being named so long before he lived?

views.label: Genuine prediction by the prophet Isaiah in the eighth century
views.case: The traditional reading holds that Isaiah, writing under inspiration, named Cyrus well in advance. This is the very kind of evidence the passage claims, that only the true God can announce events before they occur, 44:7 and 45:21. The New Testament treats the whole scroll as Isaiah's, John 12:38-41.

views.label: A later prophet writing in the exile
views.case: Many modern scholars hold that chapters 40 to 55 come from a prophet working during or near the exile, when Cyrus was already rising, and that the book was later joined into one scroll. They point to the different historical setting from chapters 1 to 39, the way the audience is addressed as exiles, and the absence of other long-range predictions with names.

debates.bearing: The chapter's own argument is about the God who foretells, and that is the thing every reader has to face. Readers who hold a single author take the claim at its strongest; those who hold a later author still have to deal with the promise that the exiles will be brought home, which Jeremiah also made. In either case the passage's message to the reader is the same: the God who speaks does what He says.

debates.question: What does 'I form light and create darkness; I bring prosperity and create calamity' mean in verse 7?

views.label: Sovereignty over every circumstance
views.case: The pairs, light and darkness, prosperity and calamity, cover everything. The Hebrew word for calamity, ra, can also be translated 'evil,' but the opposite here is shalom, well-being, which points to disaster and not to moral wrong. Amos says the same, 'If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?' Amos 3:6.

views.label: A reply to a dualistic view of the world
views.case: Some have heard in the verse a direct response to the Persian religion of the day, in which light and darkness were set against each other as opposing powers. The LORD claims both for Himself, and so no rival power can be paired with Him. This reading fits the repeated 'there is no other.'

debates.bearing: The two readings fit together, since both say that nothing in the world is outside God's rule. The text does not say that God authors sin. It says that He is Lord of both the good days and the hard ones, and so the exiles' suffering was not the work of another power.

debates.question: Who is speaking in verse 15, and what does it mean that God 'hides Himself'?

views.label: The nations' confession continues
views.case: Verse 14 ends with the foreigners saying 'God is indeed with you,' and verse 15 may be their further reflection: they have been astonished that the God of this small people is the one who saves and yet whose ways are hidden. It fits the sense that the Gentiles are marvelling at how God works.

views.label: The prophet, or Israel, speaking
views.case: Others hear a note of wonder from the prophet himself, who sees that God has been hidden through the exile, Isaiah 8:17, and has now shown Himself. The verse then expresses the awe of someone who has lived through the silence and now sees its purpose.

debates.bearing: Either speaker gives the same point. God's hiddenness is not absence, and it does not mean that He is unreachable. In the very next verses He insists that He has not spoken in secret, verse 19, so the hiddenness describes His ways, not His word.

study.originalLanguages:
The title of honour in verse 4 is a verb, akanneka, 'I have given you a title' or surname, from kana, to address by a name. The idea is that God has attached a name of dignity to Cyrus, calling him 'shepherd' in 44:28 and 'anointed' in 45:1, though he does not know the one who gave it. The verse says it twice, 'I call you by name' and 'I give you a title of honor,' and both are set against 'you have not known Me.' The word 'know,' yada, runs through the oracle: God acts 'so that you may know,' verse 3, 'so that all may know,' verse 6.

The shepherd, ro'i in 44:28, is from ra'ah, to tend or graze, the same verb that describes the idol-worshipper 'feeding' on ashes in 44:20. The word for what the shepherd will accomplish is chephets, desire or pleasure, and the verse says he will 'fulfill all that I desire,' so the shepherd's work is not his own plan but the LORD's. In the ancient Near East 'shepherd' was a stock title for a king, and Isaiah gives it to a pagan.

The grip of verse 1, 'whose right hand I have grasped,' is chazaq, the same verb as in 42:6, 'I will take hold of your hand.' It is a striking echo, since the one taken by the hand in 42:6 is the Servant. The doors that open before Cyrus, daltayim, and the gates that will not be shut are the language of a city taken without resistance.

The statement of verse 7 sets shalom, well-being, against ra, calamity, and in other contexts ra can mean moral evil, but a contrast with shalom favours calamity here. The verse uses yatsar, form, for light and bara, create, for darkness and calamity, with the plain 'make' for prosperity, and the first two verbs are the same pair as in 43:1. The Maker who forms and creates is described with the vocabulary of Genesis 1.

The ground of Cyrus's task, verse 13, is that he will free the exiles 'not for payment or reward,' lo bimchir velo veshochad. The word mechir is a price, and shochad is a bribe or gift. In 43:3 God gave nations as ransom; here He uses a king who asks for no price. The idea that the exiles could be sold for nothing and redeemed without money appears in 52:3.

In verse 15 the word 'hides Himself' is mistater, the participle of a verb for hiding or concealing. It is a rare description of the LORD, and the context of verse 19 shows that this is hiddenness of manner and not of message.

Twice God says that the earth was not created tohu, a waste, verse 18, and that He did not tell Jacob's descendants to seek Him in tohu, verse 19. The word is the same as that for formless emptiness in Genesis 1:2 and for the nothingness of idols in 44:9. The earth was formed 'to be inhabited,' lashevet, and the same word becomes the point of the whole creation.

In verse 22, 'Turn to Me and be saved,' the second verb is in a form that can be read 'let yourselves be saved,' as though salvation were something to be received. The 'oath' of verse 23 uses nishba'ti, 'I have sworn,' and the same verb yields 'swear allegiance,' so the oath that God swears by Himself calls forth an oath in return. 'A word that will not be revoked' is literally a word that will not return, which recalls Isaiah 55:11.

The last verb, 'justified,' in verse 25 comes from tsadaq, to be righteous or in the right, and the phrase 'in the LORD' says where that standing is found. It is the vocabulary Paul uses for justification by faith, Galatians 3:8.

typology.type: Cyrus the anointed shepherd who frees captives, 44:28 and 45:1
typology.fulfillment: Cyrus is the only foreign ruler to whom Isaiah gives the title anointed, and he is called to free exiles, to see Jerusalem built and to lay the temple's foundation. The correspondence with Christ is real: both are chosen by name for a rescue that they carry out on behalf of God's people. The escalation is considerable. Cyrus released captives from a foreign city, while Christ proclaims liberty to those held by sin, Luke 4:18-21. Cyrus did not know the LORD, verse 4, while Jesus knows the Father perfectly, John 10:15. And Cyrus freed the exiles at no cost to himself, verse 13, whereas Jesus redeems at the cost of His own life, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The type is only partial, since Cyrus was neither righteous nor a believer.

typology.type: The rebuilding of the city and temple, 44:28 and 45:13
typology.fulfillment: The promise that Jerusalem will be rebuilt and the temple's foundation laid was kept in a modest way under Cyrus and his successors, Ezra 3:10-11 and 6:14-15. Jesus speaks of a temple He will raise in three days, and John says that He meant His body, John 2:19-21. Paul says believers are being built together into a dwelling for God in the Spirit, with Christ as the cornerstone, Ephesians 2:19-22. The type is fulfilled in a different register: from a building of stone to a people. Even the second temple was a disappointment to those who remembered the first, Haggai 2:3, and the full answer is a city whose temple is the Lord God and the Lamb, Revelation 21:22.

typology.type: The nations bowing in chains and confessing, 45:14
typology.fulfillment: The picture of Egypt, Cush and the Sabeans coming over to Israel and confessing 'God is indeed with you' is the earliest form of a pilgrimage theme in the prophets, which Zechariah repeats, Zechariah 8:23. Paul draws on it when he describes an unbeliever falling down and saying 'God is truly among you,' 1 Corinthians 14:25. In Christ the picture changes in a crucial way: the nations come not in chains of captivity but as free people brought near, Ephesians 2:13, and what they bring into the city is their glory, Revelation 21:24. The type is partly corrected, since in Isaiah it can sound like conquest, while in Christ it is a gathering by grace.

typology.type: The oath and the bowing knee, 45:23
typology.fulfillment: God swears by Himself that every knee will bow, an oath that the writer of Hebrews takes as the model of God's unshakeable promise, Hebrews 6:13. Paul tells the Philippians that the knee will bow at the name of Jesus, Philippians 2:10-11, after the descent of the Son to a servant's form and death on a cross. The correspondence is not merely a similar scene but the same event: the universal homage owed to the LORD is given to Jesus, and it is to the glory of God the Father. The type is not outgrown but fulfilled, and Paul adds that on that day the confession will be made by those in heaven, on earth and under the earth.

study.christ:
The most explicit link is Philippians 2:9-11. Paul takes the words of Isaiah 45:23, in which the LORD swears by Himself that every knee will bow before Him and every tongue will swear allegiance, and says that God has given Jesus the name above every name, 'that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.' It is hard to overstate how bold this is. In Isaiah the oath is made precisely to exclude any rival: it follows 'there is no other' and 'I am God.' Paul, a Jew who knew the passage intimately, places Jesus in the position that the oath reserves for the LORD, and he does it without any sense that the monotheism of the passage has been broken. The glory goes to the Father, and the homage goes to the Son, because they are one God. Romans 14:11 uses the same verse with the one who will judge, 14:10, in view, so the Judge before whom all give account is Christ.

The second link is a pairing of two titles in verse 21, 'a righteous God and Savior.' A God who is both righteous and a Savior is a problem, since a righteous judge must condemn the guilty and a savior must rescue them. Paul sees the answer in the cross: God presented Christ as an atoning sacrifice, 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:25-26. The two halves of verse 21 are brought together in a single act. Titus then calls Jesus 'our great God and Savior,' Titus 2:13, which uses the language of verse 21 for Him.

The chapter's invitation, 'Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth,' verse 22, is where the New Testament's mission to the nations has its roots. Jesus' last words send the church to every nation, Matthew 28:19. When Paul says in Galatians that Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, Galatians 3:8, he is reading verses 22 and 25 together. And the promise that all Israel's descendants will be justified in the LORD, verse 25, is the Gospel's grammar: a standing that is in someone else.

Cyrus himself is a partial picture, and the passage helps explain why the early church took the title seriously. The word anointed is the word behind 'Messiah,' mashiach, and 'Christ,' christos. Cyrus is a king anointed to free captives and rebuild; the Christ is the one who frees from sin and builds a people. Where Cyrus acted for the LORD without knowing Him, Jesus acts as the Son who knows the Father, Matthew 11:27. The contrast is part of the teaching: a pagan conqueror can be an instrument, but only the Son can be the Saviour.

The statement 'I have not spoken in secret,' verse 19, is one that Jesus takes up in His trial when He says that He has spoken openly to the world and said nothing in secret, John 18:20. A caution applies: the passage is about the LORD's identity and Cyrus's commission, and not every detail, such as the gates of bronze, is a hidden picture of Christ.
study.god:
The God of this oracle is first of all the Lord of history in a sense that reaches down to individuals. He names a king before the king is born, 44:28, and He directs him, 45:2 and 45:5, so that the movement of armies and the fall of cities fall within His plan. Yet the text does not stop at power. The reason given for Cyrus's call is the people: 'For the sake of Jacob My servant and Israel My chosen one,' verse 4. The God who rules empires does so for the sake of a small and defeated nation.

He is also the God who acts without being known. 'Though you have not known Me,' He says twice. The text refuses to make His activity depend on being recognised. He equips a pagan king for battle, and the purpose of it all is that the king, and everyone else, will come to know Him. His sovereignty precedes and creates the knowledge of Himself.

His uniqueness is expressed again and again, and it is not a bare claim of numerical oneness. 'I am the LORD, and there is no other' is the voice of a God who is Creator, not one deity among many. The creation language makes this concrete: He formed light and darkness, He made the earth and created man on it, verse 12, and He formed the earth not for emptiness but to be inhabited, verse 18. Because He made things for a purpose, He does not speak 'in a wasteland,' verse 19. His speech is as purposeful as His creation.

He is a God who hides Himself, verse 15, and yet He is the one who says He has not spoken in secret. These two statements do not contradict each other. His ways may be hidden, and He may keep silent for long ages, as in 42:14, but His word is plain and public. This is a God who is neither absent nor easily manipulated.

He is righteous and Savior at once. Verse 21 holds them together, and verses 8 and 24 and 25 speak of righteousness and strength found in the LORD alone. Justice and rescue come from the same source, and so the exiles can hope for deliverance without supposing that God has overlooked their sin.

He is patient with those who rage against Him: 'All who rage against Him will come to Him and be put to shame,' verse 24. The verse is a double-edged one, since shame is a judgment, and yet 'will come to Him' is also the language of invitation. Finally, He is a God who swears by Himself, verse 23, because nothing is greater, and His oath is the pledge of a purpose that cannot fail.

For worship, the chapter asks us to stop quarrelling with the Potter and to give Him what He has sworn to receive. The proper answer to 'Turn to Me and be saved' is to turn.

crossReferences.note: The proclamation of Cyrus, issued in the first year of his reign, says that the God of heaven appointed him to build a house at Jerusalem and invites the exiles to return. The writer says the LORD stirred Cyrus's spirit to fulfil the word spoken through Jeremiah, so the decree is the historical fulfilment of what Isaiah 44:28 and 45:13 describe.

An Aramaic memorandum records Cyrus's decree about the temple, with its dimensions, the rule that costs be met from the royal treasury, and the return of the gold and silver vessels. It supplies the practical detail behind 'not for payment or reward,' Isaiah 45:13, since the exiles were given resources and not charged.

Jeremiah tells the exiles that when Babylon's seventy years are complete, God will confirm His promise to bring them home. It gives the timeline in which Isaiah 44:26 and 45:13 are fulfilled and shows that the return was promised by more than one prophet.

God says that He summons a bird of prey from the east, a man for His purpose, and that what He has planned He will do. It is a further reference to Cyrus and uses the language of purpose and planning, which fits the argument of chapter 45 that the God who declares the end also brings it about.

Paul asks who we are to talk back to God and says that the potter has the right to make from the same clay different vessels. The footnote on Isaiah 45:9 notes that this is cited in Romans 9:20, so Paul is applying the woe on those who quarrel with the Maker to his own argument about God's freedom.

Paul applies the oath of Isaiah 45:23 to Jesus: at His name every knee will bow and every tongue confess that He is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. It is the clearest case in the New Testament of a text about the LORD being used about Christ.

Paul quotes the promise that every knee will bow and every tongue confess to God and uses it to remind believers that each will give an account to God. It draws a more sober lesson from Isaiah 45:23 than Philippians does: the verse is also about judgment.

The writer says that when God made His promise to Abraham, He swore by Himself since He had no one greater to swear by. It is the same oath-by-Himself that Isaiah 45:23 declares, and it shows how the New Testament reads God's self-sworn word as the unshakeable basis of hope.

Paul says God put Christ forward as an atoning sacrifice so as to be just and to justify those who have faith in Jesus. It resolves the pairing of Isaiah 45:21, 'a righteous God and Savior,' by showing how God can be both.

Before Pilate's court Jesus says that He has spoken openly to the world and said nothing in secret. It echoes the claim of Isaiah 45:19, and places Jesus in the line of the LORD who does not speak from a land of darkness.

Ten men from every tongue grasp the robe of a Jew, saying that they have heard that God is with you. It is a later form of the confession in Isaiah 45:14 and shows that the nations' pilgrimage to a God known through His people became a lasting hope.

Paul says that Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith and announced the gospel to Abraham in advance. It matches the invitation to all the ends of the earth in Isaiah 45:22 and the justification of all the descendants of Israel in 45:25.

study.oneStory:
This passage joins the two halves of the Old Testament's hope, the calling of Israel and the blessing of the nations. In Genesis 12:3 God told Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, and for most of the Old Testament that promise is hard to see. Here it comes into plain view. The God who has been working through a small nation says to the whole world, 'Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth,' and swears by Himself that every knee will bow. The question of what the line of Abraham was for is answered in a single oath.

It also looks back to the first chapters of Genesis. The Creator who made the heavens and spread out the earth, 44:24, and who formed the earth to be inhabited, 45:18, is the God of Genesis 1, who made a world to be filled and ruled. The repeated word tohu, the waste and emptiness of Genesis 1:2, sets the idols against the creation: the idol-makers are nothing, and the earth was not made to be empty. The answer to the world's disorder is not another power from inside it but the Creator who spoke before the thing came to be.

The passage also advances the plot. The return under Cyrus ended the exile and rebuilt the temple, Ezra 1 to 6, and the book of Ezra ends with the community still small and still under foreign rule. The prophets who came after, and the Gospels, show that something larger was still waited for. The 'new things' of Isaiah, and the invitation to the nations, are carried forward by the Servant, whose work reaches to the ends of the earth, Isaiah 49:6, and then by the church, which takes the name of the one before whom every knee bows.

The story ends with that oath kept. John sees a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language standing before the throne, Revelation 7:9, and hears every creature in heaven and on earth declare praise to the one who sits on the throne and to the Lamb, Revelation 5:13. The nations walk by the light of the city, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it, Revelation 21:24. Those who once raged against Him, as verse 24 says, are met by a God who has made a way for the world to come, and the God who 'did not create it to be empty' dwells with a people who fill it.

quiz.q: What specific claim does the LORD make about Cyrus in 44:28?

options.text: That Cyrus is His shepherd who will fulfill all His purposes, including rebuilding Jerusalem and its temple.
options.note: Verse 28 states this specific naming and purpose directly, well before Cyrus's birth.

options.text: That Cyrus will become a worshiper of the LORD from birth.
options.note: The passage later says Cyrus does not know the LORD, verses 4 to 5, even though he serves God's purpose.

options.text: That Cyrus will destroy Jerusalem completely.
options.note: The opposite; Cyrus is named as the one who will see Jerusalem and the temple rebuilt, not destroyed.

options.text: That Cyrus will rule only over Persia with no wider influence.
options.note: The passage describes Cyrus subduing nations and disarming kings, far beyond ruling Persia alone.

quiz.q: What striking title is given to Cyrus in 45:1, despite his not knowing the LORD?

options.text: The LORD's anointed.
options.note: Verse 1 gives Cyrus this title, mashiach, remarkable for a pagan king.

options.text: A false prophet to be avoided.
options.note: The opposite; Cyrus is named as God's chosen instrument, not a false prophet.

options.text: An enemy of God's people to be destroyed.
options.note: The passage presents Cyrus as an instrument of deliverance for God's people, not their enemy.

options.text: A rival god to be worshiped alongside the LORD.
options.note: Cyrus is presented as a human instrument used by the one true God, not a rival deity.

quiz.q: What image does verse 9 use to describe the folly of questioning God's purposes?

options.text: Clay quarreling with the potter who shapes it.
options.note: Verse 9 uses exactly this image of the absurdity of clay questioning its maker.

options.text: A shepherd questioning his sheep.
options.note: The image used is the potter and clay, not a shepherd and sheep.

options.text: A king questioning his own soldiers.
options.note: Not the image used here, which specifically concerns a craftsman and the material he shapes.

options.text: A father questioning his own reflection.
options.note: The image given is specifically the potter and the clay he forms, illustrating the Maker-creature relationship.

quiz.q: What universal invitation closes this passage in verse 22?

options.text: Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth.
options.note: Verse 22 issues this invitation directly to every nation, not Israel alone.

options.text: Only Israel is invited to turn and be saved.
options.note: The opposite; the invitation is explicitly extended to 'all the ends of the earth.'

options.text: Salvation is limited to those who first defeat their enemies in battle.
options.note: The invitation is simply to turn to the LORD, not a military condition for salvation.

options.text: The invitation applies only to future generations, not those currently living.
options.note: The invitation is addressed directly and immediately, 'turn to Me and be saved,' not deferred to a future generation only.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament apply Isaiah 45:23, 'every knee will bow before Me'?

options.text: Paul applies it directly to Jesus, declaring every knee will bow at His name, Philippians 2:10-11.
options.note: Philippians 2:10-11 quotes this very language and applies it to Christ's lordship.

options.text: The New Testament never references this verse.
options.note: The opposite; Paul directly applies this verse to Jesus in Philippians 2, and again in Romans 14:11.

options.text: It is applied only to angelic beings, not to any human or divine figure.
options.note: Paul applies it specifically to Jesus Christ, not to angels.

options.text: It is applied only to Old Testament kings, with no New Testament significance.
options.note: Its clearest New Testament application is directly to Jesus Christ, not to Old Testament kings.

questions: The LORD names Cyrus by name more than a century before his birth. What does this level of detailed foreknowledge tell you about how much God already knows and has planned for your own life?
Cyrus served God's purposes even though he did not know the LORD personally. Where might God be using people or circumstances in your life for good, even ones that do not consciously acknowledge Him?

The image of clay questioning its potter warns against disputing God's right to direct history. Is there a decision or circumstance in your life right now where you are quarreling with your Maker instead of trusting Him?
The invitation 'turn to Me and be saved' is addressed to all the ends of the earth, not a select few. Who in your life needs to hear this open invitation from you this week?
Paul applies 'every knee will bow' directly to Jesus. How does picturing every knee, including your own, one day bowing before Christ change the way you live and worship today?

translationNotes.note: Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian Empire, conquered Babylon in 539 BC and issued a decree recorded in Ezra 1:1-4 releasing captive peoples, including the Jewish exiles, matching this prophecy's specific claims about Jerusalem and the temple.

'I form the light and create the darkness, I bring prosperity and create calamity' asserts God's sovereignty over all events without making Him the author of moral evil; the parallel term to prosperity is calamity or disaster, not moral wickedness.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture tool for Isaiah 44:24-45:25.
